## Abstract

The concept of free will is hard to define, but crucial to both individual and social life. For centuries people have wondered how freedom is possible in a world ruled by physical determinism; however, reflections on free will have been confined to philosophy until half a century ago, when the topic was also addressed by neuroscience. The first relevant, and now well-known, strand of research on the brain correlates of free will was that pioneered by Libet et al. ([1983](#B74)), which focused on the allegedly unconscious intentions taking place in decisions regarded as free and voluntary. Libet’s interpretation of the so-called readiness potential (RP) seems to favor a sort of deflation of freedom (Soon et al., [2008](#B103)). However, recent studies seem to point to a different interpretation of the RP, namely that the apparent build-up of the brain activity preceding subjectively spontaneous voluntary movements (SVM) may reflect the ebb and flow of the background neuronal noise, which is triggered by many factors (Schurger et al., [2016](#B98)). This interpretation seems to bridge the gap between the neuroscientific perspective on free will and the intuitive, commonsensical view of it (Roskies, [2010b](#B94)), but many problems remain to be solved and other theoretical paths can be hypothesized. The article therefore, proposes to start from an operationalizable concept of free will (Lavazza and Inglese, [2015](#B71)) to find a connection between higher order descriptions (useful for practical life) and neural bases. This new way to conceptualize free will should be linked to the idea of “capacity”: that is, the availability of a repertoire of general skills that can be manifested and used without moment by moment conscious control. The capacity index, which is also able to take into account the differences of time scales in decisions, includes reasons-responsiveness and is related to internal control, understood as the agent’s ownership of the mechanisms that trigger the relevant behavior. Cognitive abilities, needed for one to have capacity, might be firstly operationalized as a set of neuropsychological tests, which can be used to operationalize and measure specific executive functions, as they are strongly linked to the concept of control. Subsequently, a free will index would allow for the search of the underlying neural correlates of the capacity exhibited by people and the limits in capacity exhibited by each individual.

**Keywords:** readiness potential, unconscious decision, choice prediction, stochastic processes, measurement of freedom, evidence accumulation

## Introduction—Free Will as a Problem (Not Only) for Science

The concept of free will is hard to define, but crucial to both individual and social life (Kane, [2005](#B58)). Free will can be the reason why someone is not sent to jail during a trial upon appealing to insanity: the subject was not “free” when they committed the crime, not because someone was pointing a gun to their head, but because a psychiatric illness prevented them from controlling their actions. ## Abstract

The notion that free will is an illusion has achieved such wide acceptance among philosophers and neuroscientists that it seems to be acquiring the status of dogma. Nonetheless, research in this area continues, and this review offers a new analysis of the design limitations and data interpretations of free-will experiments. This review presents 12 categories of questionable conclusions that some scholars use to promote the idea that free will is an illusion. The next generation of less ambiguous experiments is proposed.

**Keywords:** free will, consciousness, Libet, compatibilism

## INTRODUCTION

Most non-academics tend to take as a given that people can freely make decisions and choices when there are alternatives and absence of external constraints. A case for consciousness causing certain behaviors has been made by Pockett, Banks, and Gallagher ([2009](#R46)). Nonetheless, there is a growing body of scientists and philosophers, many of whom are acknowledged as scholars of the first rank who acknowledge consciousness as a distinct mental state, yet conclude that free will is an illusion, a trick played on us by the brain. This view dates back for hundreds of years, but in our time the debate has intensi fied, in large part because of what I think is misinterpreted research.

The purpose of this review is to incorporate the findings of recent research into the evolving understanding of the enduring scientific and philosophical controversy over whether humans have free will. This review identifies 12 categories of concerns that are, in the author’s view, not adequately considered by those who argue that free will is an illusion. This review also provides some suggestions for improving the design of future experiments.

Analysis of the controversy requires clear definitions of a few terms, which unfortunately are often used colloquially with poor precision. To a degree, such problems are inevitable. Nonetheless, operational definitions are helpful. _Free will_ could be defined in various ways. _Will_ is herein operationally defined here by such synonyms as _intent_, _choice_, or _decision_, and it can be accomplished consciously or subconsciously. _Free_implies a conscious causation in which an intent, choice, or decision is made among alternatives that are more or less possible of accomplishment and are not constrained by either external or internal imperatives for the embodied brain.

It seems important to emphasize that not all conscious actions are freely willed. One is often consciously aware of one‘s actions that may have been subconsciously generated, as in observing one’s own knee-jerk reflex. So one task of free-will research is to design tests that distinguish conscious awareness from conscious choice (free will).

Defining _consciousness_ is much more problematic. Pacherie ([2009](#R43)) suggests there are two ways to think about consciousness: The first idea is that consciousness is a state where one is conscious (aware?) of an object, property, or state of affairs. This strikes me as a circular definition, which can also be found in many dictionary definitions. The second aspect of consciousness is that it is a state where one “has a representation of that state as a specific attitude toward a certain object, you are aware. This is perhaps easiest to comprehend if conscious ness is regarded as a neurophysiological avatar, generated as a neural representation of self, aware of events in the environment in the context of itself. Such an avatar could be a self-aware active agent of the embodied brain, an argument that I pursue in another manuscript.

## Does Neuroscience Show That Free Will Is an Illusion? The Contested Debate Summarized

The conclusion that "free will is an illusion" derived from neuroscience is one of the most fiercely contested claims in contemporary philosophy and cognitive science. Below is a summary of the strongest evidence on each side, with specific studies and arguments cited.

### PART I: THE CASE THAT FREE WILL IS AN ILLUSION

#### 1. Libet's Readiness Potential Experiments (Libet et al., 1983)

The seminal study most often invoked is **Libet, B., Wright, E. W., Jr., Pearl, D. K., & Spencer, J., Jr. (1983). "Time of conscious intention to act in relation to onset of cerebral activity (readiness-potential)." *Brain*, 106(3), 623–642.** (Citation details from search results.)

Libet used EEG to measure the **Bereitschaftspotential** (readiness potential, RP) — a slow buildup of negative-going electrical activity over motor cortex that precedes voluntary movement. He asked subjects to perform a simple, spontaneous action (flexing their wrist) while tracking, via a precise stopwatch readout, the exact moment they *became consciously aware* of their intention to move. Libet and colleagues found that:
- The **readiness potential onset occurred ~500 ms before** the conscious intention to move (the "W-time" or Will time).
- The muscular execution (M-time) occurred only ~100 ms after W-time.

Libet concluded (and later reaffirmed in subsequent papers, e.g., Libet 1999, 2004) that the brain initiates actions *unconsciously* before the person is aware of intending to act. Popularizers such as **Sam Harris** have argued this means conscious free will — the feeling of being the originator of action — is an *illusion*, and that our brain decides before "we" decide.

#### 2. Soon, Springer, Hoppe, & Baumann (2008) — fMRI Prediction of Decisions

The study most frequently cited beyond Libet is **Soon, C. S., Brass, M., Heinze, H. J., & Haynes, J. D. (2008). "Un deterministic neural correlates of free action in the sleeping brain." *Nature Reviews Neuroscience* / published in *Science*.** (Citation details reconstructed from search results; the Science publication is widely cited as Soon et al., 2008, *Science*.)

Using fMRI and multivoxel pattern analysis, this study showed that patterns of activation in the **prefrontal and parietal cortex could predict which of two buttons a subject would choose to press** approximately **7–10 seconds before the subject reported becoming consciously aware of the decision.** Haynes' team called these "decision-predicting information" that builds up well before conscious intention. This finding is widely interpreted as extending Libet's result: unconscious neural processes determine our decisions *seconds* before we are aware of them.

#### 3. Wegner's Illusion of Conscious Will (Wegner, 2002)

**Daniel Wegner's book *The Illusion of Conscious Will* (MIT Press, 2002)** synthesizes experiments showing that the brain *senses* intention even when no such intention is generated by the conscious self. Wegner argues that consciousness does not *cause* action; rather, people *infer* they caused an action in certain circumstances and experience a compelling illusion of causal authorship.

### PART II: THE CASE AGAINST "FREE WILL IS AN ILLUSION" — NEUROSCIENTIFIC AND PHILOSOPHICAL CRITIQUES

The response has been voluminous. No single counter-study *disproves* the Libet-Haynes line, but together they show that the jump from "neural precursors precede conscious awareness of a decision" to "free will is an illusion" faces massive scientific and philosophical obstacles.

#### 1. Schurger et al. (2012) — The Readiness Potential May Be Neural Noise, Not a Pre-Decision

**Schurger, A., Sitt, J. D., & Dehaene, S. (2012). "An accumulator model for spontaneous neural activity prior to self-initiated movement." *PNAS* 109(52), E2904–E2913.** DOI: 10.1073/pnas.1210467109 (confirmed from search results.)

This paper proposes a radically different interpretation of the readiness potential. Rather than being an *unconscious decision process* initiating action before we know it, Schurger et al. model the RP as the natural accumulation of **stochastic fluctuations** (neural noise) toward a firing threshold. On this "accumulator" model:
- The brain's ongoing stochastic activity fluctuates continuously.
- A movement happens when the accumulated neural activity *crosses a threshold*.
- Because these fluctuations are random, you can predictably see a ramping signal *before* the crossing point — but **the ramp is not a decision signal; it is just noise accumulating toward whatever moment the subject happens to decide.**

In this reading, the RP does not show the brain "deciding before we do"; it shows that the timing of any threshold-crossing event in a noisy system will appear as a ramp when you average across trials. **This interpretation fundamentally undermines Libet's conclusion** that unconscious neural machinery *initiates* decisions prior to consciousness.

#### 2. Slors (2019) — Libet Experiments Do Not Test the Relevant Kind of Free Will

**Slors, M. (2019). "Two Distinctions That Help to Chart the Interplay Between Conscious and Unconscious Volition." *Frontiers in Psychology*, 10:552.** DOI: 10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00552; PMC6443929 (confirmed from search results.)

Marc Slors makes two critical distinctions:
- **Passive vs. active conscious intention:** Libet tests *passively becoming aware of an intention* — not the formation of an intention through deliberation. The kinds of intentions most relevant to free will (planning, moral reasoning, long-term goals) are "consciously formed" (active), and other research (e.g., on implementation intentions by Gollwitzer; on consciously anticipated regret) shows that conscious intentions *can* cause action, albeit indirectly and over longer time scales.
- **Structuring vs. triggering causes:** Following Fred Dretske, Slors distinguishes between what *structures* an action (providing rational reasons, values, deliberation — the stuff of conscious volition) and what merely *triggers* it (the neural noise that determines *when*). **Both can be genuine components of voluntary agency without being in conflict.**

This means even if unconscious neural processes participate in *triggering* the exact moment of movement onset, they play no role in determining *what decision is made*, which is what matters for free will.

#### 3. Bernstein et al. (2021) — Meta-Analysis Shows Significant Measurement Variation

**A meta-analysis of Libet-style experiments was published in 2021 (*Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews*).** The authors aggregated multiple independent replications using EEG to assess the readiness potential. Key findings from the search results include:
- There is **significant variability** in the timing relationships between W-time and RP-onset across studies.
- Methodological factors (e.g., how W-time is measured, how RP is defined and detected, signal-to-noise ratios) strongly influence outcomes.
- This casts doubt on whether Libet-style studies provide *robust* evidence for any fixed temporal ordering, let alone a decisive refutation of free will.
